analysis.one_liner: Puts federal anti-manipulation oversight over previously unregulated energy derivatives trading.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2002 with four Senate Democrats behind it after the Enron collapse, the bill never received a committee vote or floor vote; it died in the Senate Agriculture Committee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would close a loophole in federal commodities law that let energy trading — futures, options, forwards, and swaps tied to electricity and natural gas — happen largely outside regulators' view. It would repeal the 'exempt commodity' category, put formerly exempt swaps under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's fraud and manipulation rules, require trading platforms to register, report, keep records, and hold capital reserves, and give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority over energy derivatives markets. It was introduced after Enron's collapse, when it became widely known that online energy trading had operated with almost no federal oversight.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity and natural gas bills, since regulators would gain the power to detect and penalize manipulation of the markets that set energy prices. Trading platforms' counterparties also gain fraud protections.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'exempt commodity' category in the Commodity Exchange Act, so that transactions previously carved out of oversight no longer escape the Commodity Futures Trading Commission entirely.
Subjects formerly exempt swap transactions to CFTC enforcement and to prohibitions on manipulating market prices, and expands the ban on fraudulent or misleading contracts.

Requires eligible electronic trading facilities to register with the CFTC, file reports, keep books and records open to CFTC and Justice Department inspection at all times, and maintain sufficient net capital.

Gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission jurisdiction over derivatives transactions based on electric energy or natural gas prices — futures, options, forwards, and swaps — and over anyone operating an electronic forum where such trades happen, and makes it unlawful to charge unjust, unreasonable, discriminatory, or preferential rates for them.

Directs FERC to meet quarterly with the CFTC, SEC, FTC, and Federal Reserve on energy trading conditions and to report annually to Congress, and allows FERC to pay market-level salaries to recruit financial and energy analysts.

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms, swap dealers, and banks that trade electricity and natural gas derivatives, who would bear registration, reporting, recordkeeping, and capital requirements and could no longer trade without anyone watching. Compliance costs could also be passed into trading costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy trading firms and swap dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not eliminate the exemption entirely: bilaterally negotiated deals between sophisticated 'eligible contract participants' that are not traded on a facility stay exempt from most of the Commodity Exchange Act, getting only anti-manipulation and fraud coverage — so a layer of the market remains dark.

Critics of derivatives oversight in that era argued that registration, reporting, and net capital requirements would raise trading costs and push some energy trading offshore or onto foreign exchanges, potentially adding to the prices American consumers pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but one-sided in the record: the cost is compliance expense borne by large trading firms and possibly passed into trading costs, while the benefit is regulators' ability to see and police markets that set retail energy prices. The main design weakness is that individually negotiated off-exchange swaps between big players remain mostly exempt, so the bill shrinks rather than closes the loophole it targets. Even so, the loophole it targets was large enough that oversight would have mattered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which is where jurisdiction over commodities law sits, and the committee never took any action on it; when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, the bill died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on February 14, 2002, with Senators Cantwell, Wyden, and Boxer as cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

The subjects on the bill include 'corporate collapse' and 'derivative securities'; it was introduced weeks after Enron's December 2001 collapse, which had exposed how energy derivatives were traded online largely outside federal oversight following a 2000 law that created the 'exempt commodity' category this bill would repeal.

The action history shows only introduction and referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote ever occurred, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 with the bill still in committee.

The oversight this bill sought did not reach over-the-counter derivatives in that Congress; comparable authority over swaps generally arrived years later, after the 2008 financial crisis, in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy trading companies and swap dealers kept operating energy derivatives markets outside CFTC anti-manipulation rules and FERC jurisdiction, and continued to avoid registration, reporting, and recordkeeping for the rest of the Congress. Ratepayers got no new protection against manipulation of the markets that set their bills.

for.name: 3 of 49 Senate Democrats

against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill, held no recorded hearing or markup, and let it remain pending until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the chamber's position is unknown; all four senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats, and no Republican is recorded as supporting it.

industries.industry: Energy trading companies and online energy trading platforms
industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to trade electricity and natural gas derivatives outside CFTC and FERC oversight, forcing registration, reporting, recordkeeping, capital reserves, and exposure to manipulation penalties. Their gain under the status quo came at ratepayers' expense, since unwatched markets set the prices consumers pay.

industries.industry: Banks and swap dealers trading energy derivatives
industries.note: Formerly exempt swaps would become subject to CFTC enforcement and anti-manipulation prohibitions, and dealers would have to file reports and keep records open to federal inspection.
The bill would grant FERC new jurisdiction over energy derivatives markets and let it pay market-comparable salaries to recruit the economists, engineers, and financial analysts needed to run them.
